title: Rice, brown and wild, cooked, no added fat

content.title: About
content.content: Brown and wild rice are whole grains that retain the bran and germ. When cooked without added fat they keep their natural flavor, aroma, and nutrients. Wild rice, although technically an aquatic grass, is higher in protein and minerals than typical rice varieties.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Brown rice contains twice as much fiber as white rice.
Wild rice was a staple for many Native American tribes and is often called “the gold of the plains.”
Cooking brown rice requires more water and a longer cooking time than white rice.
Wild rice has a lower glycemic index than most other rice types.
In Russia wild rice is sometimes referred to as “Western” or “American” rice.

items.title: High in fiber
items.content: Fiber supports digestion, promotes satiety, and helps regulate blood sugar levels.

items.title: Plant‑based protein source
items.content: Wild rice provides about 15 % protein, higher than most grains, offering a valuable amino‑acid profile for vegetarians.

items.title: Contains magnesium and phosphorus
items.content: These minerals are essential for bone health, muscle function, and nerve signaling.

items.title: Low glycemic index
items.content: Helps maintain stable blood glucose, beneficial for people with pre‑diabetes or diabetes.

items.title: Antioxidants
items.content: Brown and wild rice contain phenolic compounds that protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Arsenic content
items.content: Like most rice, brown rice can contain trace amounts of inorganic arsenic; rotating with other grains is advisable.

items.title: Digestive heaviness
items.content: The high fiber content may cause discomfort for some individuals if large portions are consumed.

items.title: Cereal allergy
items.content: Rarely, people with cereal allergies may react to rice.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Cooked brown and wild rice can be served as a side dish, added to salads, soups, vegetable stir‑fries, or used in Asian‑style recipes. It stores well in the refrigerator for up to 5 days or can be frozen for longer shelf life.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep cooked rice in an airtight container in the fridge for no more than 5 days. For extended storage, freeze portions in freezer‑safe bags at –18 °C, where they remain good for up to 3 months.
